content: Potassium sorbate is the potassium salt derived from sorbic acid. Its primary function is as a food preservative, identified by the E number 202. It is widely utilized in various applications, including food products, wine production, and personal care items. The molecular formula of potassium sorbate is C6H7O2K, and its systematic chemical name is potassium (E,E)-hexa-2,4-dienoate. It is synthesized through the chemical reaction between sorbic acid and potassium hydroxide. Potassium sorbate is commonly used to inhibit the growth of molds and yeasts in numerous food products, such as cheese, wine, yogurt, dried meats, and baked goods. It is also frequently found in the ingredient lists of dried fruit products. Additionally, herbal dietary supplements often include potassium sorbate to prevent microbial growth and extend shelf life. It is used in quantities that are considered safe, with no known adverse health effects. On product labels, it is listed as potassium sorbate. In personal care products, potassium sorbate is employed to prevent the proliferation of microorganisms, thereby enhancing product stability. Some manufacturers have adopted potassium sorbate as a substitute for parabens. In the context of wine production, it is sometimes referred to as a wine stabilizer. When added to wine, potassium sorbate produces sorbic acid, serving two key purposes. First, after active fermentation has ceased and the wine has been clarified and racked for the final time, potassium sorbate prevents any remaining yeast from reproducing. While existing yeast cells may continue fermenting residual sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol, no new yeast cells will form to initiate further fermentation. Second, when wine is sweetened prior to bottling, potassium sorbate is used in conjunction with potassium metabisulfite to prevent refermentation. This is particularly important for sweet wines, sparkling wines, and certain hard ciders, though it may also be added to wines that struggle to maintain clarity after fining. It is worth noting that some molds, such as certain strains of Trichoderma and Penicillium, as well as some yeasts, can detoxify sorbates through decarboxylation, resulting in the production of 1,3-pentadiene. This compound emits a characteristic odor reminiscent of kerosene or petroleum. From a toxicological perspective, potassium sorbate is regarded as safe due to its long-standing safety record and non-toxic profile. It is non-irritating and non-sensitizing, with allergic reactions being rare. It is also well-tolerated when consumed internally.
